Lore/Peoples/High-Elves.title: High Elves
Lore/Peoples/High-Elves.content:
High Elves


                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

A people reduced by ninety percent in a single afternoon, now scattered, addicted, and split over what to do about it.


Descendants of the Highborne exiled from Kalimdor after The Sundering. They founded Quel’Thalas and created the Sunwell from a stolen vial of the Well of Eternity. Their alliance with humanity dates to The Troll Wars, and they taught the first human mages.
In The Third War, Arthas Menethil cut the Dead Scar through their kingdom to reach the Sunwell and defiled it to raise Kel’Thuzad. Nine in ten high elves died.
The Split

Blood Elves — the majority, who took the name sin’dorei in mourning and followed Kael’thas Sunstrider through the Dark Portal to feed their arcane addiction. Offscreen at launch.
High elves proper — the remnant who refused Kael’thas. Some remain with the Alliance: survivors of Dalaran and the Kirin Tor, a delegation in Stormwind City, the rangers at Quel’Danil Lodge in The Hinterlands, and Ambermill in Silverpine Forest. Many are bitter about the Alliance’s slow response when their kingdom burned.

Arcane Withdrawal
Both branches are physically dependent on ambient arcane energy and the Sunwell is gone. The high elves endure it. The blood elves have decided to solve it, by any means.
Related
Quel’Thalas · Blood Elves · Kael’thas Sunstrider · Sylvanas Windrunner · Kirin Tor · Arcane Magic and the Well of Eternity · Playable Species at Launch

Lore/Peoples/Humans.title: Humans
Lore/Peoples/Humans.content:
Humans



                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

Short-lived, stubborn, politically incoherent, and somehow still the Alliance’s centre of gravity.


Playable: Yes · Faction: Alliance · Homeland: Elwynn Forest · Capital: Stormwind City · Leader: King Anduin Wrynn (child), Bolvar Fordragon as regent
Where They Stand
The human kingdoms of Arathor fragmented eleven centuries ago into seven states, and the last thirty years have been an unbroken run of catastrophe. Stormwind fell to the orcs and was rebuilt. Lordaeron was destroyed by its own crown prince. Alterac was dissolved for treason. Dalaran is a crater. Gilneas has sealed itself behind the Greymane Wall and stopped answering letters. Stromgarde is a contested ruin. Kul Tiras has withdrawn in fury since Admiral Proudmoore’s death.
What remains is Stormwind — ruled by a ten-year-old boy, a regent doing his honest best, and a black dragon.
How They Got Here
They were one kingdom. Arathor united the human tribes, won The Troll Wars alongside the high elves, and then did what every human polity does eventually — split into seven pieces over succession, trade, and pride.
Then the Portal opened. The First War cost them Stormwind entirely. Refugees crossed the sea to Lordaeron and were taken in, which bought a great deal of goodwill and a debt nobody has finished paying.
The Second War was their finest hour. Seven kingdoms, the dwarves, the high elves, and the newly-founded Order of the Silver Hand broke the Horde. Humans led it. They have not stopped mentioning it.
Then the rebuilding of Stormwind went wrong. The Stonemasons’ Guild rebuilt the city and the nobles refused to pay. The guild rioted, the queen died in the riot, and the survivors became the Defias Brotherhood. Every problem in Westfall traces to that unpaid bill.
Then the plague. Arthas Menethil killed his father and handed Lordaeron to the dead. Every human alive lost someone or knows someone who did.
Who Leads Them
On paper: King Anduin Wrynn, aged ten.
In practice: Bolvar Fordragon, Regent Lord — a genuinely decent paladin and soldier who is holding a kingdom together with no money and no mandate, and who is out of his depth in the council chamber.
Underneath that: the noble houses, who control the money and are not being taxed effectively, and the Church of the Holy Light, which has more moral authority than the crown and knows it.
Human politics is a scrum of institutions — guilds, orders, houses, and churches, all with charters, all citing them.
Where They Fit
Humans are the Alliance’s connective tissue. They are individually the weakest of the four peoples — no darkvision, no ten-thousand-year memory, no stonework, no clockwork — and they compensate by being the ones everybody talks through.
The Stormwind court hosts the diplomacy. Human is the trade language. When dwarves and night elves have a problem with each other, a human writes the letter.
What They Just Survived

The Third War — the northern kingdom destroyed, the Silver Hand shattered, hundreds of thousands dead or worse
The Scourge, which is still in the Plaguelands and has not gone anywhere
The Defias uprising, which is less “survived” and more “ongoing”

What They Are Fighting Now



































WhereWhoWhyWestfallDefias BrotherhoodAn unpaid debt that turned into an insurgency. The province is effectively lost.Redridge Mountains, Burning SteppesBlackrock orcsRend Blackhand’s Dark Horde never accepted the peace and is pushing eastDuskwoodThe dead, and worseSomething is wrong in that forest and nobody has the manpower to find out whatAlterac MountainsSyndicateDispossessed Alterac nobles turned banditHillsbrad FoothillsForsakenA slow, ugly border war that nobody has declared
What They Want
Stormwind wants to stop bleeding. Pay the army, hold the provinces, get through the winter. That is genuinely the whole agenda and it is not being achieved.
The refugees want Lordaeron back, which is not possible, and some of them have not accepted that. The Scarlet Crusade is what happens to that grief when it curdles.
The Church wants a Highlord, or at least an answer to what happened to Arthas. The Order of the Silver Hand has not replaced Uther and cannot agree on what it now stands for.
The nobles want their rents.
Character Traits

Adaptable — the only species with mages, paladins, priests, warriors, warlocks, and rogues
Short memory, long grudges — three generations is ancient history, but the Defias debt is unforgiven
Institutional — humans build guilds, orders, churches, and bureaucracies compulsively
Diplomatic by necessity — they are the weakest individually and know it

How They Talk
Plain, formal in public, and full of Light-language even from people who do not attend services.





































PhraseWhen”Light be with you.”Greeting, farewell, and reflex. Said to strangers and enemies alike.”By the Light—“Surprise, exasperation, mild swearing”For Stormwind!”Battle cry. Increasingly said with something to prove.”Nine copper a day.”A soldier’s grumble. The army’s pay, and shorthand for being taken for granted.”That’s a Lordaeron problem.”Once meant someone else’s problem. Now it lands like a slap, and people still say it without thinking.”Long live the king.”Correct, required, and awkward. He is ten.”Ashes to Andorhal.”Newer, grimmer. Said of anything past saving.
What They Make of the Others


                  
                  Not symmetrical, on purpose 
                  
                

How a people sees its neighbours rarely matches how those neighbours see them. The gaps are where the roleplay is.


Dwarves — The warmest thing the Alliance has. Two generations of shared trenches, and a debt to Ironforge that Stormwind’s treasury will not be settling soon. Humans find dwarves restful — they say what they mean and they buy their round.
Gnomes — Fond bewilderment. Nobody quite follows what a gnome is explaining, and everybody wants them nearby when something breaks. The tendency to treat a catastrophe as an interesting result unsettles people who lost a house to one.
Night Elves — Awe, and a persistent sense of being judged. They are older than the kingdom, they gave up more than anyone to win the last war, and they clearly find humans exhausting. Four years in, most humans still have not spoken to one.
Orcs — The wound. They burned Stormwind, and there are men alive who carried children out of it. The official position is that the Horde has changed; the position in the taverns is that a generation of atrocity does not wash out because a warchief says so.
Forsaken — Horror, and it is specific. These were Lordaeron — neighbours, congregations, families. A human meeting a Forsaken is not meeting a monster, they are meeting somebody who might know their mother’s name, and that is worse.
Tauren — Almost no contact. What filters back through Theramore says patient, honest, and slow to anger, which is inconvenient for anyone who needs the Horde to be simple.
Darkspear Trolls — Trolls sacked Arathor’s borders for two centuries and human histories have not forgiven it. That the Darkspear had nothing to do with any of that is a distinction few people make and fewer care about.
Playing One
The default outsider’s-eye view of Azeroth — the species that has to have things explained to it, which makes it the easiest entry point for a player learning the setting.
Five different characters, five different campaigns:

Stormwind loyalist — army, guard, or church. You have a chain of command and it is failing you.
Lordaeron refugee — you had a life and a country and now you have neither. Where you put that grief is the character. The Scarlet Crusade is recruiting, and you know it.
Westfall local — you grew up with the people who became Defias. You are one bad winter from being one of them, and you know their names.
Kul Tiran sailor — your admiral died at Theramore and your nation blames Jaina Proudmoore for it. You may or may not agree.
Alterac exile — your kingdom was dissolved for treason before you were born and you have been living it down ever since.

Questions worth answering at session zero: Who did you lose in the plague? Do you attend services, and does the Light answer you? Are you being paid, and by whom?
Related
Stormwind City · Anduin Wrynn · Bolvar Fordragon · The Holy Light · Defias Brotherhood · Lordaeron · Order of the Silver Hand · A Short History of Azeroth

Lore/Peoples/Kobolds.title: Kobolds
Lore/Peoples/Kobolds.content:
Kobolds


                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

“You no take candle!”


Small, rat-like, candle-wearing subterranean scavengers who infest every mine on the Eastern Kingdoms. Cowardly individually, dangerous in the dark and in numbers.
They are the first thing most adventurers ever kill, and vanilla’s most quotable enemy. Found in Elwynn Forest (Fargodeep and Jasperlode mines), Dun Morogh, Redridge Mountains, and essentially any hole in the ground.
Related
Elwynn Forest · Dun Morogh · Bestiary MOC

Lore/Peoples/Murlocs.title: Murlocs
Lore/Peoples/Murlocs.content:
Murlocs


                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

Amphibious, incomprehensible, and they always, always bring friends.


Bipedal fish-people infesting every coastline, lake, and marsh on both continents. Their language is untranslated. Their society is unstudied. Their aggression is total.
Notable for two things: the noise (an unmistakable gurgling shriek that means at least four more are coming), and the fact that they were the immediate threat driving the Darkspear Trolls to extinction before Thrall intervened.
Related
Darkspear Trolls · Westfall · Darkshore · Dustwallow Marsh

Lore/Peoples/Naga.title: Naga
Lore/Peoples/Naga.content:
Naga


                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

Queen Azshara’s drowned court, ten thousand years underwater, and they have not gotten over it.


When The Sundering pulled the Kaldorei capital beneath the sea, Queen Azshara and her Highborne struck a bargain with a power in the deep — almost certainly an Old God — and were transformed into serpentine immortals.
They have spent ten millennia in the Maelstrom. They are now, for the first time, coming back up.
Where They Surface at Launch
Darkshore · Azshara (the zone) · Desolace (Sar’theris Strand) · Stranglethorn Vale (the Cape) · Blackfathom Deeps · Feralas (Isle of Dread) · Dustwallow Marsh


                  
                  What they want is not clear 
                  
                

Naga incursions at launch look like raids and reconnaissance rather than invasion. Lady Vashj has taken a large contingent to Outland to serve Illidan Stormrage. What Azshara herself wants is unknown and unknowable in 2004 — she has not been seen.


They surface in places naga have no business being, and nobody on either coast can explain the pattern.
Related
Queen Azshara · Azshara (zone) · The Sundering · Blackfathom Deeps · Darkshore · The Old Gods · Lady Vashj

Lore/Peoples/Night-Elves.title: Night Elves
Lore/Peoples/Night-Elves.content:
Night Elves



                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

Ten thousand years of immortality, spent four winters ago to kill one demon. They are still processing it.


Playable: Yes · Faction: Alliance · Homeland: Teldrassil · Capital: Darnassus · Leader: High Priestess Tyrande Whisperwind
Where They Stand
The Kaldorei survived The Sundering by withdrawing from the world entirely — ten millennia of isolation in Ashenvale and beyond, guarding Nordrassil, sleeping in barrow dens, and forgetting how to negotiate.
Then The Third War came to their door, and they detonated their World Tree to destroy Archimonde.
How They Got Here
They had an empire. Around the Well of Eternity, ten thousand years ago, and by their own admission it was magnificent and it was rotten. Their queen’s court opened a door for the Legion.
The War of the Ancients nearly ended them. They won. The Well exploded, the continent broke, and the survivors crawled out onto a changed world with a permanent horror of arcane magic.
Then they stopped. Ten thousand years in the forests of Ashenvale and Darkshore: druids sleeping in the barrow dens, Sentinels awake and watching, nothing changing, nobody visiting. Immortality made this seem reasonable.
The Third War restarted the clock. Orcs cut into Ashenvale, Cenarius was killed, the Legion arrived, and the kaldorei found themselves fighting alongside people they had spent a war’s worth of effort trying to expel.
Then they burned Nordrassil to kill Archimonde, and woke up mortal.
Four years ago they grew Teldrassil — a new World Tree off the north coast — and joined the Alliance. Both decisions were made fast, by a small number of people, and are being second-guessed daily.
Who Leads Them
Tyrande Whisperwind, High Priestess of Elune, rules — and rules alone, which is not the arrangement anyone planned.

Malfurion Stormrage, her partner and the first druid, is lost in The Emerald Dream. His body sleeps. Nobody will say for how long.
Fandral Staghelm runs the Cenarion Circle in Malfurion’s absence. He grew Teldrassil against the Dragon Aspects’ advice and refused their blessing. He lost his son at The War of the Shifting Sands and something in him did not come back.
The Sentinels answer to Tyrande and are the actual instrument of kaldorei policy.
The Wardens — the jailers — are largely elsewhere, chasing an escapee. See Illidan Stormrage.

Society is matriarchal. The Sentinels (military) and the Sisters of Elune (priesthood) are women’s institutions. The Cenarion Circle was men’s until very recently. Both arrangements are now under strain, because a mortal people cannot afford to keep half its population out of any role.
Where They Fit
Awkwardly, and recently. The Alliance is four years old to them — an eyeblink — and they joined it because Jaina Proudmoore’s people fought beside them at Mount Hyjal, not because they like humans.
They bring the Alliance the entire western continent, an unmatched scouting corps, and the Cenarion Circle — which is also full of Tauren, and therefore constitutes the only warm cross-faction relationship in the world.
They also bring an absolute prohibition on arcane magic and a view of Ashenvale logging as desecration rather than trade, which makes them a difficult ally at exactly the points where the Alliance would like to be flexible.
What They Just Survived

The loss of immortality — chosen, collective, and not yet grieved
The Third War, Cenarius’s death, and the burning of Nordrassil
Illidan’s release after ten thousand years of imprisonment, and his escape

What They Are Fighting Now



































WhereWhoWhyAshenvaleWarsong orcsLogging. To the Horde a supply line; to the kaldorei a desecration on the site of Cenarius’s death.Darkshore, AshenvaleCorrupted FurbolgOld allies driven mad. This one genuinely grieves them.Felwood, JaedenarSatyr, and worseLegion residue that never left, in a forest that is visibly dyingAzsharaNagaTheir own exiled kin, returned from the sea after ten thousand yearsTeldrassilSomethingThe tree took root without a blessing. The druids are not saying more than that.
What They Want
Tyrande wants the world put back, which is not on offer, and is settling for holding Kalimdor.
The Cenarion Circle wants Felwood cleansed and the Dream made safe, and is short-handed because half its membership is still asleep in the barrow dens.
Ordinary kaldorei want to know how long they have. Nobody has told them what a mortal night elf’s lifespan is, because nobody knows. It is the question underneath every other question.
A quiet faction wants out of the Alliance and back into isolation, and it is growing.
Character Traits

Xenophobic, and working on it — the Alliance is four years old and feels like a compromise
Deeply hostile to arcane magic — it destroyed their empire. Mage is not a night elf option and that is policy.
Ecological absolutism — Horde logging in Ashenvale is not a trade dispute, it is desecration
Patient to the point of paralysis — a decade is a short time to consider something

How They Talk
Formal, unhurried, and full of moon-language. Darnassian phrases survive in common speech even when kaldorei are speaking to outsiders, and they rarely bother to translate.









































PhraseMeaning”Ishnu-alah.”Well fortune to you. The standard greeting.”Ishnu-dal-dieb.”Good fortune to you. The standard reply.”Elune-adore.”Elune be with you. Warmer, more devout.”Ande’thoras-ethil.”May your troubles be diminished. A farewell, and what you say to the bereaved.”Bandu thoribas.”Prepare to fight. A formal challenge, not a threat.”Ash karath!”Get it done. A Sentinel’s order.”Thero’shan.”Honoured student. Its pair, shan’do, means honoured teacher. Both are earned.”In a hundred years it will not matter.”Was wisdom. Has recently become a very dark joke.
What They Make of the Others


                  
                  Not symmetrical, on purpose 
                  
                

How a people sees its neighbours rarely matches how those neighbours see them. The gaps are where the roleplay is.


Humans — Children who have not stopped moving long enough to learn anything. There is real gratitude for Hyjal underneath it, and real bafflement that a people who live sixty years behave as though they have all the time there is.
Dwarves — Tolerable until they start digging. The kaldorei view is that some things were buried by people who knew what they were doing, and that the Explorers’ League has never once asked whether it should.
Gnomes — The machines are an offence. The gnomes themselves are almost impossible to dislike, which the kaldorei find irritating in a way they have not resolved.
Orcs — Ashenvale. Cenarius. They cut the forest where he died and they are still cutting. Whatever the orcs say about blood curses and freedom, a demigod is dead and the axes have not stopped.
Forsaken — Obscene. Not evil — obscene. Death is part of the cycle and these things have stepped out of it and kept walking, and the kaldorei have no framework that makes room for that.
Tauren — The surprise of the age. Cenarius took tauren students, the Circle took tauren partners, and the warmest relationship the night elves have is with a people on the other side of the line.
Darkspear Trolls — The thing nobody says aloud. The kaldorei rose from troll stock in the deep past, every troll alive knows it, and a night elf asked directly will change the subject with great composure.
Playing One
The best night elf PCs are the ones caught between eras — old enough to remember the world before, young enough to have to live in the one after.
Four shapes worth taking:

Sentinel — you fought at Mount Hyjal and you cannot understand why the war did not end when you won it
Awakened druid — you went into the barrow den before The Third War and came out after it. Your people are mortal. Nobody warned you.
Young kaldorei — born within the last century, which makes you a child. You have never known immortality and find the elders’ grief slightly self-indulgent, which you would never say aloud.
Doubter — a scholar or priestess who thinks Staghelm was wrong about Teldrassil and cannot get anyone senior to listen

Questions worth answering at session zero: How old are you, and how has that changed? Were you awake for The Third War? What do you actually think of the Alliance — and of humans specifically, who live sixty years and act as though they have time?
Related
Teldrassil · Darnassus · Tyrande Whisperwind · Malfurion Stormrage · Fandral Staghelm · Cenarion Circle · The Emerald Dream · The Sundering · Ashenvale · Elune · A Short History of Azeroth

Lore/Peoples/Ogres.title: Ogres
Lore/Peoples/Ogres.content:
Ogres


                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

Draenor’s other export. Big, stupid, occasionally two-headed, and occasionally the smartest thing in the room.


Ogres came to Azeroth with the orcish Horde through the Dark Portal, and stayed after it lost. Some remain allied to orcish remnants; most have gone feral and set up as bandits and warlords.
Ogre magi — often two-headed — are the exception: intelligent, spellcasting, and dangerous. The Gordunni in Feralas are the most organized.
Where They Are
Feralas (Gordunni) · Arathi Highlands (Boulderfist) · Alterac Mountains (Crushridge) · Dustwallow Marsh (Brackenwall — Horde-allied) · Blasted Lands (Dreadmaul) · Stranglethorn Vale (Mosh’Ogg) · Burning Steppes · Dire Maul (post-launch)
Related
Feralas · Dustwallow Marsh · Arathi Highlands · Goblins · Dark Portal

Lore/Peoples/Orcs.title: Orcs
Lore/Peoples/Orcs.content:
Orcs



                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

A people who were made into a weapon, used, discarded, caged, and who are now — for the first time in three generations — free and sober and trying to work out who they actually are.


Playable: Yes · Faction: Horde · Homeland: Durotar · Capital: Orgrimmar · Leader: Warchief Thrall
Where They Stand
Orcs are not from Azeroth. They are from Draenor, where they were shamanic clan-people until Kil’jaeden and Gul’dan fed them Mannoroth’s blood and turned them into an army. The red skin, the rage, the atrocities of the First and Second Wars — all of it was the curse.
Grom Hellscream broke it. At Demon Fall Canyon in Ashenvale, he drank the demon blood one final time to gain the strength to kill Mannoroth — and killed the curse with him. He died doing it. Orc skin has been fading from red toward brown ever since, and orcish children born since are the first free generation in living memory.
How They Got Here
They were clans, not a nation. Frostwolf, Warsong, Blackrock, Bleeding Hollow, Shattered Hand and the rest — herders, hunters, and shaman on the plains of Draenor, at peace with the draenei until they were not.
Gul’dan sold them. In exchange for power he delivered his entire people to the Legion. The clans drank, the shamans went deaf to the elements, and the Horde was born as a weapon aimed at another world.
The First War and The Second War — through the Portal, Stormwind destroyed, the northern kingdoms invaded, and finally broken by the Alliance at Blackrock Spire. Orcs did those things. Every orc alive knows it.
Then twenty years in the camps. Not fighting — lethargy. Cut off from the demon blood, most orcs simply stopped: no fight, no work, no interest. A generation was born behind fences.
Thrall emptied them. Born in captivity, raised as a human noble’s gladiator, escaped, found the Frostwolf clan and Drek’Thar, and learned the shamanism his people had lost.
Then he left. Rather than continue the war, Thrall took his people west across the sea to a continent nobody had claimed, and fought at Mount Hyjal alongside the humans and night elves on the way.
Who Leads Them
Warchief Thrall — young, extremely capable, and carrying more moral authority than any leader on either side. He is shaman first and warchief second, and that ordering annoys a number of his generals.
Beneath him:

The clan chieftains, who retain real independence. Frostwolf loyalty is personal to Thrall; Warsong loyalty is complicated and lives in Ashenvale.
The shaman, rebuilt almost from nothing, who advise and are listened to
The Kor’kron, Thrall’s own guard, which is newer than the city they patrol

Orgrimmar is four years old and built of raw timber and iron. It looks temporary because it is.
Where They Fit
The orcs are the Horde, in the sense that they founded it and hold the capital — but the modern Horde is a coalition of the dispossessed, and the orcs are the only members who arrived as conquerors rather than as refugees.


                  
                  This Horde is not that Horde 
                  
                

It includes Tauren, Darkspear Trolls, and the Forsaken. It is a coalition of the dispossessed, not a war machine. Thrall genuinely wants peace with the Alliance. Almost nobody in the Alliance believes him, and a significant number of orcs think he’s gone soft.


That gap — between what the Horde is now and what everyone remembers it being — is the central political fact of orcish life.
What They Just Survived

The demon blood, and its breaking, and the fact that it was one of their own who paid for it
Twenty years of internment — see The Interbellum
The Third War and the crossing to Kalimdor
Founding a country from nothing, four years ago, in a desert

What They Are Fighting Now



































WhereWhoWhyAshenvaleNight elf SentinelsWarsong logging. The Horde calls it supply; the kaldorei call it desecration on the spot where Cenarius died.Blackrock MountainRend Blackhand’s Dark HordeOrcs who never accepted Thrall, still demon-tainted, still fighting the old warDurotar, OrgrimmarBurning BladeA fel cult recruiting orcs who miss the strength the blood gave themStonetalon Mountains, The BarrensAlliance outposts, Venture CompanyResources, territory, and a border war nobody has declaredHillsbrad FoothillsThe AllianceOfficially not happening
What They Want
Thrall wants legitimacy. Not conquest — recognition. A homeland that is accepted as a homeland, and a peace that survives him.
The old guard wants the war back, or at least wants to stop apologising. There is a real constituency for the view that Thrall has confused honour with weakness.
Ordinary orcs want the settlement to hold. Durotar is hard ground, the harvests are poor, and the question of whether a warrior people can feed itself by farming is not rhetorical.
Everyone wants the shamanic tradition restored properly, and everyone knows they are one generation of teachers away from losing it again.
Character Traits

Honour is the organising principle — lok’tar ogar, victory or death, but honourably
Shamanism restored — a spiritual practice deliberately rebuilt from near-extinction
Deeply defensive about the past — every orc knows what their fathers did
Blunt — orcish culture prizes directness to a degree other species find alarming

How They Talk
Direct to the point of rudeness by human standards, and full of Orcish loanwords that orcs do not translate for outsiders. Formality is reserved for oaths and for the dead.









































PhraseMeaning”Lok’tar ogar!”Victory or death. The oldest one, and it predates the demon blood.”Throm-ka.”Well met. The standard greeting between orcs.”Zug zug.”Sure. Fine. On it. Casual assent. Deeply informal.”Dabu.”I obey. Said to a superior, and meant.”Aka’magosh.”A blessing — roughly good will and honour go with you. Said on parting, and at gravesides.”Lok’narash!”Arm yourselves.”Strength and honour.”The everyday version. Said the way humans say take care.”Blood and thunder!”Old, aggressive, and a bit embarrassing now. The elders still use it.
What They Make of the Others


                  
                  Not symmetrical, on purpose 
                  
                

How a people sees its neighbours rarely matches how those neighbours see them. The gaps are where the roleplay is.


Humans — Complicated in a way that no orc enjoys explaining. They caged a generation, and one of them raised Thrall. Both facts are true and neither cancels the other.
Dwarves — Honest enemies, met on open ground, no poison and no tricks. That earns respect and stops well short of warmth.
Night Elves — They will not let Ashenvale go, and a growing number of orcs privately think they are entitled not to. Grom’s death bought the whole people their freedom, and it also killed a god in someone else’s forest.
Gnomes — Never fought them and cannot quite work out what they are for. The machinery is interesting; the volume is not.
Forsaken — Useful, watched, and never fully trusted. Thrall took them in because turning away a homeless people is what was done to the orcs, and every orc understands the reasoning without necessarily liking the result.
Tauren — The debt. The tauren taught the orcs shamanism back after the Legion took it, and asked for nothing. There is no orc who will speak against them.
Darkspear Trolls — The first people on this continent who chose to stand with the Horde rather than being conquered into it. The voodoo makes some orcs uneasy and none of them raise it.
Playing One
The central orc question is what a warrior culture does when the war is over — and every good orc PC is some answer to it.
Five shapes worth taking:

Frostwolf — Thrall’s own clan, shaman-heavy, loyal to the man rather than the office. You were never in a camp because your clan was never caught.
Warsong veteran — you fought in Ashenvale and you are not sorry. Grom was your chieftain and he died a hero, whatever the elves say.
Camp-born — you were born behind a fence and freed as a child. You have no memory of the old Horde and are quietly impatient with everyone else’s guilt.
Shaman — you are part of a revival four years old. Your grandparents would not recognise what you are doing.
Old guard — you fought in The Second War under the blood. You are sober now and you dream about it.

Questions worth answering at session zero: Were you in a camp? What did your father do in the wars, and do you know the details? Do you think Thrall is right?
Related
Thrall · Orgrimmar · Durotar · Grom Hellscream · Mannoroth · The Elemental Planes · Burning Blade · The Interbellum · The Horde · A Short History of Azeroth

Lore/Peoples/Quilboar.title: Quilboar
Lore/Peoples/Quilboar.content:
Quilboar


                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

Boar-men grown from the blood of a slain demigod, defending shrines nobody else considers sacred.


The quilboar sprang from the corpse of Agamaggan, the great boar demigod who died fighting the Burning Legion in The War of the Ancients. Where his blood fell, thorns grew — and from the thorns, quilboar.
They hold the razorfen thickets of the Barrens and are aggressively territorial.

























TribeWhereDeath’s HeadRazorfen Downs — now overrun by the Scourge and the lich Amnennar the ColdbringerRazorfenRazorfen Kraul, under the ancient Charlga RazorflankRazormaneDurotar, BarrensBristlebackMulgore, Barrens


                  
                  Not simply monsters 
                  
                

The quilboar are defending a holy site from grave-robbers, and the grave-robbers are the player characters. Razorfen Downs in particular is a tragedy — the Death’s Head tribe were losing to the Scourge and turned to necromancy to survive it.


Related
Razorfen Kraul · Razorfen Downs · The Barrens · Scourge

Lore/Peoples/Satyr.title: Satyr
Lore/Peoples/Satyr.content:
Satyr


                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

Night elves who accepted Sargeras’s offer, and got exactly what they asked for.


During The War of the Ancients, some Highborne swore themselves to the Burning Legion and were transformed into demonic satyrs. The first and greatest was Xavius, Azshara’s counselor.
They have persisted for ten thousand years, and they are the Night Elves’ most personal shame — because every satyr was once kin.
Where They Are
Ashenvale (Xavian, the Shrine of Aessina) · Felwood (Jaedenar, Shatter Scar Vale) · Azshara (Legash Encampment) · Desolace · Feralas · Darkshore
They practice fel magic, keep Furbolg and night elf captives, and are usually found working toward some larger demonic project — most notably at Jaedenar in Felwood, where they serve the Shadow Council.
Related
Night Elves · The Burning Legion · Felwood · Ashenvale · Shadow Council · The War of the Ancients

Lore/Peoples/Silithid.title: Silithid
Lore/Peoples/Silithid.content:
Silithid


                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

Insectoid horrors that are neither animals nor an infestation, but an army — and their masters are still sealed under the sand.


The silithid are the drone-caste of the buried empire of Ahn’Qiraj, servants of the Old God C’Thun. They erupted once before, in The War of the Shifting Sands, and were sealed behind the Scarab Wall.
They are seeping out again through hive mounds across the southern deserts.
Where
Silithus (Hive’Ashi, Hive’Regal, Hive’Zora) · Tanaris (the Gaping Chasm) · Un’Goro Crater (the Slithering Scar) · Thousand Needles
Above the drones sit the qiraji — intelligent, armored, and directing. Above them, C’Thun.
Related
Ahn’Qiraj · C’Thun · Silithus · Twilight’s Hammer · The War of the Shifting Sands

Lore/Peoples/Tauren.title: Tauren
Lore/Peoples/Tauren.content:
Tauren



                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

The Horde’s conscience — a nomadic people who just stopped being nomadic, and who are the only faction leadership in the world that everyone trusts.


Playable: Yes · Faction: Horde · Homeland: Mulgore · Capital: Thunder Bluff · Leader: High Chieftain Cairne Bloodhoof
Where They Stand
The tauren were scattered nomads hunted across the Barrens by the Centaur until Thrall’s orcs helped Cairne Bloodhoof drive them off. Cairne repaid that debt by bringing his people into the Horde, and has never once regretted it — though he has frequently disagreed with it.
Thunder Bluff on the mesas of Mulgore is four years old and is already the most peaceful place on either continent. It is neutral ground where even Alliance emissaries have been received.
How They Got Here
They were always here. Tauren predate every other civilisation on Kalimdor except the night elves, and their oral history reaches back past The Sundering to a time when they hunted a much larger world.
Then the Centaur came. Born, the tauren say, of a violated earth-spirit — and the centaur have hunted tauren for centuries with the specific intent of exterminating them. This is not a border dispute. It is the defining fact of tauren history.
They went nomadic to survive it. Not by choice. A people that does not settle cannot be besieged, and for generations the tauren simply kept moving.
Then Thrall’s fleet arrived. The orcs met Cairne’s people mid-migration, helped them break a centaur host, and asked for nothing. Cairne has been repaying that ever since.
Then they stopped walking. Thunder Bluff is the first permanent tauren settlement in living memory, and there is an entire generation growing up in it who have never migrated. Their elders find this wonderful and slightly worrying.
And Cenarius taught them. The night elves’ demigod took tauren students, and the first tauren druids in history are alive right now — with no elders to ask, because they are the elders.
Who Leads Them
High Chieftain Cairne Bloodhoof — old, enormous, and the most respected individual alive on either side of the line.
Tauren governance is tribal and consultative. Cairne leads the Bloodhoof tribe and speaks for the whole people, but the other tribes are not his subjects — Runetotem, Skychaser, Ragetotem, Winterhoof, Wildmane, Grimtotem. Chieftains speak, elders are heard at length, and decisions take as long as they take.
The spiritwalkers and druids hold parallel authority that has nothing to do with the chieftains. A tauren with a vision outranks a tauren with an argument.
Where They Fit
The tauren are the Horde’s legitimacy. When Thrall needs to demonstrate that his Horde is not the old one, he points at Thunder Bluff — a city with no walls, that takes in refugees, and that has hosted Alliance envoys without incident.
They also hold the Horde’s moral line internally. Cairne objected to the Forsaken joining and was overruled, and he has kept objecting. The tauren are the only people in either faction with the standing to tell a warchief he is wrong and be listened to.
Through the Cenarion Circle they maintain the one genuinely warm cross-faction relationship in the world, with the night elf druids — which is quietly the most important diplomatic channel that exists.
The Cairne Question
Cairne is the only leader in the world who is on speaking terms with almost everyone — Thrall’s mentor, respected by Jaina Proudmoore, honoured by the night elf druids, and the one voice who consistently objected to the Forsaken joining the Horde. He is the campaign’s best neutral arbiter.
What They Just Survived

Near-extinction at centaur hands, within living memory
The end of the migration — a whole way of life set down four years ago
The Third War and the crossing into a Horde they had no part in creating

What They Are Fighting Now



































WhereWhoWhyDesolace, Thousand NeedlesCentaurThe old war. It has never stopped and it will not be settled.The Barrens, MulgoreQuilboarRazorfen raids on the herds and the roadsThe Barrens, Stonetalon MountainsVenture CompanyGoblin strip-mining. To the tauren this is not commerce, it is a wound.InternallyThe GrimtotemNot open war. Yet.MulgoreHarpies, gnollsPersistent, local, and a young warrior’s first proper fight
What They Want
Cairne wants the Horde to be worth belonging to. He did not sign his people up to a war machine and says so, repeatedly, in council.
The tauren want the herd to endure — which now means a city, which is new, and which nobody is quite sure how to defend if it comes to it.
The druids want to learn faster. Cenarius is dead, the Cenarion Circle is short-handed, and a people who have had druids for four years are being asked to help heal a continent.
The Grimtotem want the tauren back, on their terms, without orcs.
Character Traits

Deliberate — tauren do not hurry, and find it strange that others do
Honour the kill — hunting is sacramental; waste is obscene
Communal — the tribe decides, elders are heard, individuals matter less
Physically enormous — tauren are the largest playable people and rooms are built wrong for them

How They Talk
Slow, formal, and full of the land. Tauren use fewer words than anyone else and mean all of them. Interrupting a tauren is a serious rudeness, which other peoples do constantly without noticing.





































PhraseWhen”Aho.”Greeting. Also acknowledgement, agreement, and I hear you. Enormously flexible.”Walk with the Earthmother.”Farewell. The full form is may the Earthmother walk with you and yours.”An’she rises.”The sun — one of the Earthmother’s eyes. Said at dawn and about anything getting better.”Mu’sha weeps.”The moon, the other eye. Said of grief.”Do not waste what you take.”The first thing a tauren child is taught. Said as a rebuke to strangers, often.”The herd endures.”Said at funerals, and after defeats”I will consider it.”Genuinely means I will consider it, for days. Other peoples hear a no.
What They Make of the Others


                  
                  Not symmetrical, on purpose 
                  
                

How a people sees its neighbours rarely matches how those neighbours see them. The gaps are where the roleplay is.


Humans — Few tauren have met one. The accounts that come back through Theramore describe a people who are brave, badly led, and frightened, which the elders find sad rather than threatening.
Dwarves — They would understand us within a day if they ever put the shovel down. A people who honour their ancestors and work stone are not strangers.
Night Elves — Teachers, and then friends. Cenarius took our first druids and the Circle takes our elders as equals. Whatever the two Hordes and Alliances decide, that will hold.
Gnomes — Loud, generous, and building things the earth did not ask for. A tauren will listen to a gnome explain for as long as the gnome needs, which gnomes find remarkable.
Orcs — They found us mid-migration, broke a centaur host for us, and asked for nothing. Cairne repaid it with a people, and he has never once called it a mistake.
Forsaken — The one thing the tauren have consistently objected to and been consistently overruled on. Nobody in Thunder Bluff pretends this is settled.
Darkspear Trolls — Quiet, funny, and carrying more grief than they let on. The only people in the Horde who have been guests as long as the tauren were nomads.
Playing One
Tauren PCs are natural mediators and natural druids, and the species that most easily justifies being the party’s moral centre without being a scold about it.
Five shapes worth taking:

Hunter of the Bloodhoof — you took the Rite of Strength, you killed a Bristleback chief, and nothing since has frightened you as much
First-generation druid — among the first druids your people have ever produced. There is no elder to ask. You are the elder now, at nineteen.
Spiritwalker or elder’s student — you speak to ancestors, and they are not always helpful
Grimtotem who disagrees with Magatha — your tribe is drifting toward something and you can see it. Nobody outside will believe you are not part of it.
Born in Thunder Bluff — you have never migrated. The elders talk about the walk like it was holy, and you are quietly glad you missed it.

Questions worth answering at session zero: Which tribe? Did you walk, or were you born in the city? What did the centaur take from your family — because they took something.
Related
Cairne Bloodhoof · Thunder Bluff · Mulgore · Cenarion Circle · Magatha Grimtotem · Centaur · Thrall · Cenarius · A Short History of Azeroth

Lore/Peoples/Trolls.title: Trolls
Lore/Peoples/Trolls.content:
Trolls


                  
                  In a sentence 
                  
                

The first civilization on Azeroth, and every ruin you have ever looted used to be theirs.


Troll empires — the Gurubashi in the south, the Amani in the north, the Drakkari in Northrend, the Zandalari presiding over all of them — covered Azeroth before elves, before humans, before dwarves. Everything since has been decline.
Trolls are ferociously regenerative, practice voodoo and loa-worship, and hold grudges measured in millennia.
Tribes at Launch


















































TribeWhereDispositionDarkspearDurotarHorde. The exception.AmaniEastern Plaguelands, Zul’AmanHostileGurubashiStranglethorn ValeHostile. Fractured. Some worship Hakkar the Soulflayer.Atal’aiSwamp of SorrowsHostile. They hold the Sunken Temple and admit no one.SandfuryTanarisHostile. Zul’Farrak.WitherbarkArathi HighlandsHostileVilebranchThe HinterlandsHostile. Jintha’Alor.FrostmaneDun MoroghHostile. Starving.
